title: An-Nazi'at: Musa, again
hook: go to Pharaoh, he has transgressed, and ask, would you purify yourself (79:17–19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nazi'at, and souls drawn out, some hard, some gently. Your line was gently drawn.

The boss who humiliates people in meetings. The relative who only hears himself. Being sent to someone like that with a message he won't want usually means rehearsing a speech or a fight. The Qur'an tells the story of Musa, Moses, in more than one surah, and early on this path you followed him as far as the fire in the valley of Tuwa. In An-Nazi'at he comes back, briefly, sent to a hard listener indeed: Pharaoh, a king who calls himself a god. And the first thing Musa is told to say isn't a threat. It's a question.
screen: `A HARD PERSON TO TALK TO.` → `A KING WHO CALLS HIMSELF A GOD.` → `MUSA, AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Verse fifteen asks: has the story of Musa reached you? His Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa: go to Pharaoh; he has transgressed. And say to him, verse eighteen: would you like to purify yourself? And I will guide you to your Lord, so you'll hold Him in awe. An invitation, in the form of a question, to a ruler who will soon call himself lord. The verb is tazakka, from the root z-k-y. You've met that root twice on this stretch: in Ash-Shams, successful is the one who purifies the soul, and in Al-A'la, successful is the one who purifies himself. Now a word from the same root is offered to Pharaoh. Even he is invited to the thing that makes a soul succeed. In Surah Ta-Ha, Musa and his brother Harun are told the same in other words: speak to him gently, perhaps he will remember or fear. Then Musa shows him the great sign. Pharaoh denies, turns away, gathers his people, and proclaims: I am your lord, the most high. Al-a'la, the very word from the surah two weeks back. A man claiming the title of the Most High. And he is seized. The surah ends the story: in this is a lesson for whoever holds God in awe. It's the end of a week, too: the sun wrapped and the buried girl given her question; the frown, the food, the day each person flees; souls gently drawn; and now a question offered to a tyrant. Nobody, the surah suggests, is beyond being asked.
screen: `THE SACRED VALLEY OF TUWA.` · `A QUESTION, NOT A THREAT.` · `TAZAKKA — OFFERED EVEN TO PHARAOH.` · `I AM YOUR LORD THE MOST HIGH.` · then, large: `WOULD YOU PURIFY YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you find hard to talk to: not the worst person in the world, just someone where every conversation goes badly. Picture opening the next one with a real question instead of a point, like: what would help? How are you, really? Choose the words.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, Surah seventy-nine, where Musa is sent to Pharaoh with a question. Today's word.
Your line: would you purify yourself. Even a tyrant was offered a question first. Day two hundred seventeen, done.

howItsDone: Muslims read Musa's mission to Pharaoh as a model of calling others with gentle speech, following the instruction in Ta-Ha to speak to him gently.

fork.setup: you are Musa, sent to a king who calls himself a god. what are you told to say first?
fork.reveal: would you purify yourself, and I will guide you to your Lord (79:18–19). the tyrant is offered the same success as anyone.

original.note: Arabic: "purify yourself," from z-k-y, the root of zakat, offered to Pharaoh in 79:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses confronts Pharaoh.
what it means: Musa's first words to the tyrant are an invitation: would you purify yourself, and let me guide you to your Lord?

what a scholar hears: commentators hear hal laka ila an tazakka as phrased with great courtesy, like would you care to; Tuwa appears also in 20:12; Pharaoh's rabbukum al-a'la in 79:24 echoes al-a'la of 87:1.

sources.ref: Qur'an 79:15–26 (Musa at Tuwa; would you purify yourself; I am your lord the most high; a lesson for whoever fears)
